title: The honeyball
hookLine: Mahakaccana explains a short teaching: how perception spins out into endless thoughts (MN 18)

cards: A Sakyan named Dandapani, whose name means stick-in-hand, comes strolling up to the Buddha, leaning on his walking stick, and asks: what's your teaching? The Buddha answers in a sentence or two.
Dandapani shakes his head, wags his tongue, raises his eyebrows until his forehead wrinkles in three lines, and walks off, still leaning on his stick. Some teachings don't land the first time.

teach.b: MN 18, the Madhupindika. That evening, the Buddha repeats the short, dense teaching to his monks, about how perceptions and notions shaped by mental proliferation press in on a person, and goes into his dwelling.

The monks look at each other: what did he mean? They go to Mahakaccana, a monk known for unpacking brief sayings, and he lays it out step by step. Dependent on the eye and a form, eye-consciousness arises.
The meeting of the three is contact.
With contact, there's feeling. What you feel, you perceive. What you perceive, you think about.
What you think about, you proliferate. And from that, a cloud of perceptions and notions, about past, present and future, presses in.
The Pali word is papanca: spreading out, proliferation. A friend doesn't reply to a message, and five minutes later you've written their whole side of an argument they've never had.
The monks take this back to the Buddha, who says: Mahakaccana is wise; I would have explained it the same way.
And Ananda says: it's like a hungry man who finds a honeyball, a honey cake; wherever he tastes it, it's sweet. What is this teaching called?

Remember it, says the Buddha, as the Honeyball. And so a week closes: the stained cloth, effacement, Sariputta's sixteen rounds, the lion's roar, pleasure seen whole, the stony field, and the honeyball.

how: Theravada teachers often use Mahakaccana's sequence in MN 18 to explain how experience becomes thought; many meditators practice noticing contact and feeling before thinking takes over.

o: a monk's alms bowl filled with honey cakes
a teaching on how one sight spreads into many thoughts
a sweet offered to the Buddha after his meal

s: he says he would have explained it the same way.
in the chain, thinking comes before feeling
contact, then feeling, then perceiving, then thinking, then proliferating.
the teaching's name comes from Ananda's comparison
sweet wherever you taste it, like a honeyball.

games.q: the Buddha gives a short, puzzling teaching and goes inside. you're one of the monks. what do they do?
o: go to Mahakaccana and ask him to unpack it
games.why: they go to Mahakaccana, known for opening up brief sayings. his explanation is so good the Buddha says he'd have given the same one.

practice: Wait for a thought, any thought, and watch what it does next: does it bring a friend, a plan, a memory, a what-if? When one becomes three, just say inside, quietly: spreading.
Then come back to the breath and the body, to contact, before the story.

wordCard.voice: The honeyball. Mahakaccana's step-by-step map of how one sight or sound spreads into endless thoughts.

orig.note: Pali papañca: proliferation, spreading out; how one perception multiplies into many thoughts.

carryVoice: Your line: the thoughts multiply. It starts with one plain sight or sound. That's the week, and day four hundred thirteen.
